title: Developing New Leadership Habits in Low-Risk Environments
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece offers a practical method for leaders trying to build a new behavior that doesn't come naturally to them. It explains why new habits are hard to sustain — they feel inauthentic at first, others resist the change because they prefer consistency, and initial attempts are clumsy — and then lays out a sequencing strategy for overcoming that resistance. The core recommendation is to deliberately practice the new behavior first in low-stakes situations and trusted relationships, where mistakes carry little cost, before attempting it in higher-stakes settings where more is on the line. The article frames this staged approach, combined with repetition, as the realistic path to a new habit actually taking hold.
points: The essay supplies a specific sequencing strategy — practice low-risk first, then escalate — rather than simply telling leaders to 'work on' a new habit.
It identifies a social dynamic that undermines habit change that leaders often overlook: colleagues actively (if unconsciously) resist new behaviors because they prefer consistency.
It suggests explicitly forecasting the new behavior to trusted colleagues and asking for feedback, turning private practice into a supported process.
It ties habit formation to leadership outcomes broadly, framing habits as the mechanism through which almost everything a leader accomplishes gets done.
quotes: Most new behaviors are uncomfortable, especially at first. Because the new behavior is not how we typically engage, it feels inauthentic.

Others notice that as well and often resist whichever habit we are trying to create. People prefer consistency from leaders and usually fail to reward a new leadership behavior before it becomes commonplace.
Chief among these choices is to master the new behavior in low-consequence situations.
In some highly trusted relationships, leaders can even forecast to others what behavior they are attempting to master and ask for help, feedback, or both.
The leader’s habits determine almost everything they accomplish or fail to accomplish, especially with people.
